 Tackling Model Bias via Game-theoretic Multi-agent Collaboration Framework
                        for Hateful Meme Classification

                   Yiwei Wei1 Zhengliang Guo2 Shaozu Yuan3 Chengyin Hu2 *
          Zhiyang Jia2 Jiujiang Guo5 * Meng Chen4 Peiying Wang3 Longbiao Wang1,6 *

                          Abstract
Hateful meme classification aims to identify memes con-
taining hateful content and has become increasingly im-
portant in the era of social media dominance. Large mul-
timodal models (LMMs) have significantly enhanced the
understanding of multimodal content, advancing this field.
However, cognitive biases in LMMs can impede effective
collaboration among models. To tackle this issue, we intro-
duce GECO, a Game-theoretic multi-agEnt Collaboration
framewOrk that organizes multiple LMMs into interacting
agents and employs game-theoretic principles to guide them
toward an optimal cooperative equilibrium. GECO further
integrates a mixed bonus scheme with both individual accu-
racy and cross-model agreement, which together drive the
system toward a consistent cooperative solution. In addi-
tion, we implement efficient policy learning and introduce a
penalty coefficient to optimize the framework effectively and
ensure training stability. Extensive experiments on five pub-
                                                                          Figure 1. Illustration of model bias in Hateful Meme Classifica-
lic datasets demonstrate that our framework achieves new                  tion. For the hateful meme (“nikki haley . . . last”), three LMMs
state-of-the-art performance. We release our code.†                       (Qwen, Gemma, LLaVA) present varied interpretations. Within
                                                                          the game, only Gemma, having provided the correct interpretation,
                                                                          received the highest bonus, thereby guiding the entire cooperative
1. Introduction                                                           framework towards the accurate answer.

social polarization, disrupts public discourse, and leads to              trained vision-language models [21, 26] and fine-tuning
significant physical and psychological harm [13, 32]. Con-                lightweight, task-specific classifiers on top of these back-
sequently, the importance of Hateful Meme Classification                  bones. Due to the advanced reasoning capabilities of large
[37], which aims to detect hateful emotions within multi-                 multimodal models (LMMs), LMM-based methods have
modal content, has become increasingly pronounced. Ear-                   been widely adopted for hateful meme classification. Some
lier studies [46, 51] addressed this task by leveraging pre-              efforts focus on enhancing a single LMM’s performance
